notes.title: Rational numbers
notes.answer: A rational number is any number that can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.
notes.explanation: Whole numbers, fractions, terminating decimals and recurring decimals are all rational, because each can be written as a fraction of two integers.
examples: 7 is rational because 7 = 7/1. So is 1.2, because 1.2 = 12/10 = 6/5.
steps: To show 0.75 is rational, write it as a fraction: 0.75 = 75/100.
Simplify: divide top and bottom by 25 to get 3/4.
3 and 4 are integers and 4 ≠ 0, so 0.75 is rational.

notes.title: Irrational numbers
notes.answer: An irrational number cannot be written as p/q with integers p and q (q ≠ 0). Its decimal goes on forever without repeating.
notes.explanation: The square root of any whole number that is not a perfect square is irrational. π is irrational too.
examples: √9 is NOT irrational, because √9 = 3, which is rational.
steps: To decide whether √n is irrational, check whether n is a perfect square (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …).
If it is, √n is a whole number, so it is rational. Example: √16 = 4.
If it is not, √n is irrational. Example: 7 is not a perfect square, so √7 is irrational.

notes.title: Terminating and recurring decimals
notes.answer: A terminating decimal ends (0.375). A recurring decimal repeats a block of digits forever (0.333…). Both are rational.
notes.explanation: A fraction in lowest terms has a terminating decimal only when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. A decimal that never ends and never repeats is irrational.
examples: 1/7 = 0.142857142857… recurs with a block of 6 digits.
steps: Write the fraction in lowest terms.
Find the prime factors of the denominator.
If the only prime factors are 2 and 5, the decimal terminates. Otherwise it recurs.
Example: 7/20 → 20 = 2 × 2 × 5, so it terminates (0.35). 5/6 → 6 = 2 × 3, so it recurs (0.8333…).

notes.title: Recurring decimal to fraction
notes.answer: Call the decimal x, multiply by 10 (or 100) to move one repeating block past the point, subtract, and solve for x.
notes.explanation: Subtracting makes the endless repeating part cancel, leaving a simple equation.
steps: Multiply by 10: 10x = 7.777…

notes.title: Real numbers
notes.answer: Real numbers are all the rational and irrational numbers together. Every real number is a point on the number line.
notes.explanation: Natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, fractions and surds such as √2 are all real numbers.
examples: −3, 0, 2/5, √2 and π are all real numbers.
√(−4) is not a real number, because no real number squared gives −4.
steps: Classify −8: it equals −8/1, so it is rational (and an integer).
Classify 0.6: it equals 6/10 = 3/5, so it is rational.
Classify √11: 11 is not a perfect square, so √11 is irrational.
All three are real numbers.
notes.checkQuestion: Is every integer a real number?

notes.title: Commutative property
notes.answer: Commutative property: changing the order does not change the result. a + b = b + a and a × b = b × a.
notes.explanation: It holds for addition and multiplication of real numbers, but not for subtraction or division.
examples: 3 × 7 = 7 × 3 = 21. But 5 − 2 ≠ 2 − 5, so subtraction is not commutative.
steps: Look at what changed between the two sides.
If only the order of the numbers changed, it is the commutative property.
Example: 2 + √3 = √3 + 2 → the order changed → commutative property of addition.

notes.title: Associative property
notes.answer: Associative property: changing the grouping does not change the result. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (ab)c = a(bc).
notes.explanation: The numbers stay in the same order; only the brackets move.
steps: Check that the numbers are in the same order on both sides.
If only the brackets moved, it is the associative property.

notes.title: Distributive property
notes.answer: Distributive property: multiplication spreads over addition. a(b + c) = ab + ac.
notes.explanation: Multiply the number outside the bracket by each term inside, then add.
steps: To verify 5(2 + 6) = 5·2 + 5·6, work out the left side: 5 × 8 = 40.
Work out the right side: 10 + 30 = 40.
Both sides are 40, so the property holds.

notes.title: Identity and inverse
notes.answer: The additive identity is 0 and the multiplicative identity is 1. The additive inverse of a is −a. The multiplicative inverse of a (a ≠ 0) is 1/a.
notes.explanation: An identity leaves a number unchanged: a + 0 = a and a × 1 = a. An inverse brings you back to the identity: a + (−a) = 0 and a × 1/a = 1.
examples: The additive inverse of −7 is 7, because −7 + 7 = 0.
The multiplicative inverse of 2/3 is 3/2, because 2/3 × 3/2 = 1. Zero has no multiplicative inverse.
steps: For 5, the additive inverse is the number that adds to give 0: −5.
The multiplicative inverse is the number that multiplies to give 1: 1/5.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the multiplicative inverse of 4?

notes.title: Closure property
notes.answer: Closure property: the sum and the product of two real numbers are always real numbers.
notes.explanation: A set is closed under an operation when the result always stays inside the set.
examples: Natural numbers are not closed under subtraction: 3 − 5 = −2 is not a natural number.
steps: Pick any two numbers from the set.
Do the operation.
If the answer is always in the same set, the set is closed under that operation.
notes.checkQuestion: Is the sum of two real numbers always a real number?

notes.title: Simplifying square roots
notes.answer: To simplify √n, take out the largest perfect-square factor: √(a² × b) = a√b.
notes.explanation: Split the number into a perfect square times what is left, then take the square root of the perfect square.
steps: To simplify √50, find the largest perfect square that divides 50: it is 25.

notes.title: Proof that √2 is irrational
notes.answer: We prove it by contradiction: assume √2 is rational and show this leads to something impossible.
notes.explanation: If √2 were a fraction in lowest terms, both the top and the bottom would have to be even, which a fraction in lowest terms cannot be.
examples: The same method proves √3 is irrational, using divisibility by 3.
It does not work for √4, because √4 = 2 = 2/1 really is rational.
steps: Assume √2 = p/q, where p and q are integers with no common factor and q ≠ 0.
Square both sides: 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q².
So p² is even, which means p is even. Write p = 2k.
Substitute: (2k)² = 2q², so 4k² = 2q² and q² = 2k². So q is even too.
Then p and q are both even, so they share the factor 2. This contradicts step 1.
So the assumption is false: √2 is irrational.
notes.checkQuestion: In the proof, why must p be even?
